nkp.access.console: You are user{UserNum}. Sign in to the NKP console as this user. {DashboardUrl} Accept the self-signed certificate, choose Log in with ntnxlab.local, and use your credentials. Do not add the domain to your username.
nkp.deploy.intro:
Let's deploy your first app: a small NGINX web server.
In Kubernetes, a <white>Deployment</white> keeps your app running and restarts it if it ever crashes.
<input/>
nkp.deploy.cmd: In your terminal, run: kubectl create deployment user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app --image=nginx:1.27
nkp.deploy.result: Check on it any time with: kubectl get deployments When user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app shows as ready, you are done here.
nkp.service.intro:
Your app runs, but nothing can reach it yet.
A <white>Service</white> gives it a stable network endpoint. We'll start with a <white>NodePort</white>, which opens a port on every node.
<input/>
nkp.service.cmd: Expose the app: kubectl expose deployment/user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app --type="NodePort" --port 80 Find the assigned port with: kubectl get service user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app
nkp.service.result:
Browse to  http://<any-node-ip>:<nodePort>  and you'll see the NGINX welcome page.
<image src='nginx_chrome.7d0cd40e.png' alt='The default NGINX welcome page reached through the NodePort service.'/>
nkp.ingress.intro:
NodePort works, but production traffic uses a friendly hostname over HTTPS.
That's an <white>Ingress</white>, handled here by the <white>kommander-traefik</white> controller.
<input/>
nkp.ingress.yaml:
Create a file <white>simple-app-ingress.yaml</white>. It defines an Ingress:
  host:  <white>user{UserNum}.<ingress-lb-ip>.sslip.io</white>
  class: <white>kommander-traefik</white>
  backend: your service on port 80
<input/>
nkp.ingress.apply: Apply it: kubectl apply -f simple-app-ingress.yaml Then open https://user{UserNum}.<ingress-lb-ip>.sslip.io
nkp.lb.intro:
A third way to expose an app is a <white>LoadBalancer</white> service.
It gets its own external IP from <white>MetalLB</white>, no hostname needed.
<input/>
nkp.lb.cmd: Switch your service over: kubectl patch service user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
nkp.lb.result: Watch for the external IP: kubectl get service user{UserNum}-nkp-simple-app When EXTERNAL-IP is filled in, browse to it.
nkp.mt.intro:
Now a little platform thinking.
A cluster is shared by many teams, so NKP keeps them apart.
<white>Projects</white> give soft isolation (namespaces).
<white>Workspaces</white> give hard isolation across clusters.
<input/>
nkp.mt.diagram:
Here is how the scopes nest:
<image src='multitenancy_diagram.2923c533.png' alt='NKP scopes: Global, Workspaces, and Projects.'/>
nkp.project.intro:
Let's create <white>your</white> project.
It gives you a dedicated namespace named <white>user{UserNum}</white> on the workload cluster.
<input/>
nkp.project.form:
In the NKP console: Default Workspace, then Projects, then <white>Create Project</white>.
  Name and ID / Namespace:  <white>user{UserNum}</white>
  Clusters:  <white>Manually Selected Clusters</white>, pick <white>workload01</white> only
Then Continue to Project.
<image src='project_create_02.39ccb846.png' alt='The Create Project form with name, namespace, and cluster selection.'/>
<input/>
nkp.project.done: You now own the <white>user{UserNum}</white> namespace on <white>workload01</white>.
nkp.ws.intro:
A quick look at the level above projects: the <white>Workspace</white>.
It groups clusters and shows their health, cost, and projects.
<input/>
nkp.ws.explore:
Open Global, then Workspaces, then Default Workspace, and have a look around.
<image src='workspace_dashboard.a5f37201.png' alt='The Default Workspace dashboard.'/>
nkp.storage.intro:
Time for real storage.
Apps that keep data (like a database) need <white>persistent storage</white>.
NKP ships the Nutanix CSI driver, so Kubernetes can ask Nutanix for volumes automatically.
<input/>
nkp.storage.diagram:
We'll build the classic pairing: a MySQL database on <white>block</white> storage (Nutanix Volumes), which WordPress will later use.
<image src='wordpress_diagram.59a9a0b6.png' alt='WordPress frontend with a MySQL backend on persistent storage.'/>
nkp.sc.intro:
Open the <white>Kubernetes Dashboard</white> for workload01.
In your project: Clusters, the workload01 menu, then Kubernetes. Re-authenticate and accept the certificate.
<input/>
nkp.sc.namespace:
At the top, change the namespace to <white>user{UserNum}</white>.
You'll see there are no resources yet. This clean, private space is yours.
<image src='k8s_dashboard_ns.03dd6ac1.gif' alt='Selecting your user namespace in the Kubernetes Dashboard.'/>
<input/>
nkp.sc.classes:
Under Config and Storage, open Storage Classes.
<white>nutanix-volume</white> is the default (block, ReadWriteOnce). Your storage requests use it unless you say otherwise.
<image src='k8s_dashboard_sc.3bb5f540.png' alt='The StorageClasses list showing nutanix-volume as default.'/>
nkp.block.intro:
Your first stateful workload.
You'll deploy MySQL. It asks for a 20Gi volume through a <white>PersistentVolumeClaim</white>.
Since no StorageClass is named, the default <white>nutanix-volume</white> catches the request and Nutanix provisions a real volume.
<input/>
nkp.block.manifest: With namespace user{UserNum} selected, click the + in the dashboard, paste this manifest, and Upload: apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: mysql-pass type: Opaque stringData: password: nutanix/4u --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: wordpress-mysql labels: app: wordpress spec: ports: - port: 3306 selector: app: wordpress tier: mysql clusterIP: None --- apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: mysql-pv-claim labels: app: wordpress spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 20Gi --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: wordpress-mysql labels: app: wordpress spec: selector: matchLabels: app: wordpress tier: mysql strategy: type: Recreate template: metadata: labels: app: wordpress tier: mysql spec: containers: - image: mysql:8.0 name: mysql env: - name: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: mysql-pass key: password - name: MYSQL_DATABASE value: wordpress - name: MYSQL_USER value: wordpress - name: MYSQL_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: mysql-pass key: password ports: - containerPort: 3306 name: mysql volumeMounts: - name: mysql-persistent-storage mountPath: /var/lib/mysql volumes: - name: mysql-persistent-storage persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: mysql-pv-claim
nkp.block.apply:
Wait for the workloads to go green. The PVC <white>mysql-pv-claim</white> should become <white>Bound</white>.
<image src='k8s_dashboard_mysql.666d915b.png' alt='Pasting the MySQL manifest into the dashboard and uploading it.'/>
<image src='k8s_dashboard_mysql_status.2470fe92.png' alt='The MySQL workloads showing green, healthy status.'/>
<input/>
nkp.block.prompt: When your MySQL is running and the PVC is Bound, type Ok to verify: <input var='Ok'/>
nkp.welcome.intro:
Welcome to the NKP Fundamentals lab.
You will deploy an app, expose it, and give it real storage on a shared Nutanix Kubernetes Platform cluster.
No prior Kubernetes needed. We go one small step at a time, and you press Enter to move on when you are ready.
<input/>
nkp.welcome.prompt:
Your instructor assigned you a user number (user01, user02, ...).
Enter just the number: <input var='UserNum'/>
